clue.text: Side of the brain having no blood circulation

indicators.note: blood in circulation moves round and round, so the letters are sent round into a new order

parts.note: all twenty-one letters of these five words are the material

explanation.surface: A grisly medical note about part of the brain that has lost its blood supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Side of the brain' reads as a hemisphere, but 'Side' alone is the definition: a football team, here the club from the south-coast city of Brighton and Hove.
explanation.definitionFit: In British sport a side is a team, and this is the full name of the football club based on the English south coast.

clue.text: To hurry for a plane, race on a motorbike

definitions.meaning: first meaning: what fighter pilots do when ordered to rush to their aircraft and take off
second meaning: a motorcycle race over rough cross-country ground

explanation.surface: Someone racing to the airport on a motorbike to catch a flight.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is RAF slang for an urgent take-off order and also the name of off-road motorcycle racing, also called motocross.

clue.text: You'll get not very far in Finchley

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the place name, tucked within its letters

parts.note: letters two to five of the place name

explanation.surface: A grumble that you won't get far travelling around Finchley, a district of north London.
explanation.walkthrough: Finchley is a suburb of north London; the joke is that the short distance is literally inside its name.
explanation.definitionFit: An inch is a tiny unit of length, so moving one is barely moving any distance at all.

clue.text: Brave and strong, not entirely like Van Gogh

parts.note: f, short for forte, is the musical marking for loud or strong
the painter famously cut off (part of) one ear, so he was only partly without ears

explanation.surface: A description of a bold, sturdy person who somewhat resembles Van Gogh.
explanation.walkthrough: Van Gogh lost only one ear, which is why the clue says 'not entirely': he was partly earless.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone brave has no fear, which is exactly what the adjective describes.

clue.text: Drive right, right becomes left at the end

indicators.note: one letter turns into another, so a letter is swapped out here

parts.note: right in the sense of correct or fitting
R is the standard abbreviation for right
L is the abbreviation for left, placed in the final position

explanation.surface: Driving instructions about keeping right, then switching to the left at the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: Take PROPER and change its last letter, R for right, into L for left: PROPEL.
explanation.definitionFit: To propel something is to drive or push it forward, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: 21-man's croak, we hear?

parts.note: surface reading: the harsh, rasping voice of a man from France
setter's reading: Frenchmen are jokingly called frogs, so a frog's croak would be the French word for a man, the form of address you hear in France

explanation.surface: Listening to a hoarse Frenchman speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 is FRENCH, so this is a French man; 'frog' is slang for a Frenchman, and his croak is imagined as the polite title he uses.
explanation.definitionFit: Monsieur is the French title for a man, equivalent to Mr or sir, the word a French speaker would use in address.

clue.text: See 1
Strip shown in scene and suspicious motive involved

indicators.note: involved means wrapped up within, so one piece is held inside the other
something suspicious is fishy or not straight, so the letters are not to be taken in their given order

parts.note: ten letters to be rearranged and then split around the other piece
a motive or motif in music or art is a recurring theme

explanation.surface: A film or play scene in which a suspicious motive is at play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strip' is a comic strip: Dennis the Menace is the mischievous boy of Britain's Beano comic (not the American character of the same name).
explanation.definitionFit: Dennis the Menace is a long-running comic strip, so the title stands for the strip itself.

clue.text: For example, Peter Ustinov can: true or false?

indicators.note: a false version is not the true arrangement, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A quiz question asking whether Peter Ustinov is capable of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Ustinov was a British actor famous for his witty anecdotes on chat shows; he is given as an example of the type.
explanation.definitionFit: A raconteur is a skilled teller of stories, and Ustinov was a celebrated instance of one.

clue.text: Hardy casually removing lead from dog

indicators.note: the lead of a word is its first letter, which is taken away here

parts.note: a breed of sheepdog

explanation.surface: A tough-sounding person, Hardy, taking the leash off a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy is Oliver Hardy of Laurel and Hardy, known informally as Ollie; 'removing lead' reads as unclipping a leash but means dropping the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ollie is the casual short form of Oliver, the first name of the comedian Oliver Hardy.

clue.text: 8's dog tooth

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the pet of the comic character at 8 down
second meaning: an informal word for a tooth

explanation.definitionFit: Dennis the Menace's wire-haired dog in the Beano is named Gnasher, and gnashers is slang for teeth.

clue.text: Fruit's zest

definitions.note: passion fruit; the answer is the first word of its name
definitions.meaning: first meaning: as in the tropical ... fruit
second meaning: great enthusiasm or eagerness

explanation.surface: Zest reads as citrus peel, a natural thing for a fruit to have.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zest' tempts as lemon peel to go with 'Fruit'; here it means gusto.
explanation.definitionFit: Passion is strong enthusiasm, the same as zest for life, and it also names the passion fruit.

clue.text: Potato sound in the orchestra

definitions.note: describes the answer, a noun: an instrument found in the orchestra

indicators.note: the sound of a word is how it is said, so its spoken form is wanted

parts.note: a potato is a tuber, an underground stem; in non-rhotic British speech the two words are said alike

explanation.surface: A puzzling image of a potato making a noise among the orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuba is the large low brass instrument found at the back of a symphony orchestra.

clue.text: Sport, we learn, isn't made up (not Wimbledon's premier)

indicators.note: something made up is invented or composed, so these letters are put together anew
not means without, so that letter is taken out of the material

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

indicators.note: the premier item is the first one, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the initial of the tennis venue

explanation.surface: We're told some sport is genuine, not invented, and not the Wimbledon kind.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the W from WE LEARN ISNT and rearrange the rest. Real tennis is the old indoor court game from which lawn tennis, Wimbledon's game, descends.
explanation.definitionFit: Real tennis is an ancient racket game played in an enclosed court, so it is a sport.

clue.text: Causes irritation with eyes?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: annoys or provokes someone

definitions.note: describes the answer, a noun: things with eyes
definitions.meaning: second meaning: sewing implements, each with a hole called an eye

explanation.surface: Something that makes your eyes sore and itchy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eyes' suggests sore eyes; the eye is the hole in a sewing tool through which thread passes.
explanation.definitionFit: To needle is to goad or annoy, and sewing needles each have an eye for the thread.

clue.text: Libertine 1 : Harlot 0 (abandoned)

indicators.note: something abandoned is let loose and runs wild, so the letters break out of their order

parts.note: the numeral one looks like the letter I
taken as written
zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A football-style score line, Libertine one, Harlot nil, in a game that was called off.
explanation.walkthrough: Abandoned matches are a sporting idea, but here the word signals a rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lothario is a seducer of women, named after a rake in an eighteenth-century play, so a libertine.

clue.text: Paul, perhaps, threw wobbly — blimey!

parts.note: Paul is a saint, abbreviated St

indicators.note: a wobbly thing is unsteady and shaken up, so the following letters are jumbled

parts.note: five letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Paul, perhaps the setter himself, lost his temper, prompting a cry of surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul is this puzzle's setter, which makes the surface self-referential, but the wordplay wants St Paul.
explanation.definitionFit: Strewth is an exclamation of surprise or dismay, as is blimey; both are mild British oaths.

clue.text: Harshness evident and almost all see the truth

indicators.note: almost all of a word is every letter but the final one

parts.note: taken as written, then shortened
verity is a formal word for truth

explanation.surface: A harsh situation becomes plain when nearly everyone faces the truth.
explanation.definitionFit: Severity is sternness or strictness of treatment, which is what harshness means.

clue.text: Colleague's pain heard over collapse of market

definitions.note: the clue's 's means is, joining the definition

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the cry is read backwards

parts.note: the cry heard from someone in pain

indicators.note: a collapse leaves things in a heap, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A colleague is heard groaning after a stock market crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' here describes a sound one hears, the yelp, rather than signalling a soundalike.
explanation.definitionFit: A workmate is someone you work alongside, which is what a colleague is.

clue.text: 5 down from 10 may be routine

parts.note: surface reading: an arithmetic clue, or a cross-reference to 5 down and 10 across
setter's reading: counting down from ten, the numbers run from the next one to five, and those office hours describe a dull daily routine

explanation.surface: It looks like a grid cross-reference or a simple sum.
explanation.walkthrough: The numbers mimic references to other clues, but neither 5 down nor 10 across is involved.
explanation.definitionFit: Nine to five is the standard office working day, so the phrase stands for an ordinary routine job.

clue.text: Settle for some honest leadership

indicators.note: some means a portion, so the answer is part of the following words

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Settling for a bit of straightforward leadership.
explanation.definitionFit: To nestle is to settle down snugly and comfortably, a near synonym of settle in.

clue.text: Expletive to be pardoned could be "knickers"

definitions.meaning: first meaning: from the phrase used to excuse swearing
second meaning: a style of loose, wide-legged women's underwear

explanation.surface: Someone apologising after swearing, 'knickers!' being a mild British curse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knickers!' is a mild British exclamation of annoyance, which makes it look like the expletive; it is the underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: People say 'pardon my French' after swearing, and French knickers are a recognised style of lingerie.

clue.text: Shop around for transport

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a mart is a market or shop

explanation.surface: Shopping around for a means of getting about.
explanation.definitionFit: A tram is a passenger vehicle running on street rails, a form of public transport.

clue.text: One unwillingly held underwear with mark inside

indicators.note: inside places one piece within the other

parts.note: hose are stockings or tights
a tag is a label or identifying mark

explanation.surface: A garment label stuck inside some underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: A hostage is a captive kept against their will as security for a demand.

clue.text: Regarding Enigmatist being only half-drunk: therapy's required

parts.note: re means regarding or concerning

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about, so these letters lurch out of order
only half a word survives, so the back half is cut away

parts.note: the name of a fellow crossword setter, taken as written then halved

explanation.surface: A worry that fellow setter Enigmatist is tipsy and needs treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: Enigmatist is another Guardian setter; keep the first five letters of his ten-letter name and rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: A regimen is a prescribed course of diet, exercise or treatment, the kind of plan therapy involves.

clue.text: Eat Chinaman up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up reads the word from bottom to top

parts.note: a common Chinese surname, used here to stand for a Chinese man; the term is now considered offensive

explanation.surface: A dated, now offensive instruction to eat a Chinese man up.
explanation.definitionFit: To gnaw is to eat by persistent biting and chewing, a particular kind of eating.

clue.text: Virtually repugnant, 51 hair-like projections

indicators.note: virtually means nearly but not quite, so the last letter is lost

parts.note: vile means disgusting
51 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A description of fifty-one disgusting little hairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Villi are the tiny finger-like outgrowths lining the small intestine, fine projections resembling hairs.

clue.text: Purgative offered when Moggy car hit Rolls

parts.note: moggy is British slang for a cat

indicators.note: something that rolls tumbles over, so these letters tumble into a new order

parts.note: six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cat struck by a car and a Rolls-Royce, a cleansing experience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolls' looks like a Rolls-Royce that hit the cat, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathartic is a laxative medicine that purges the bowels, so a purgative.
